articles.title: They fell in love on The Simpsons and married in real life. Meet the French Homer and Marge
articles.summary: They have brought TV’s most famous cartoon couple to life in France for the last 38 years. Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau tell all about working and living together for so long, still being lovebirds – and rarely arguing.
body: The Simpsons is the biggest cartoon comedy in the world, with suburban couple Homer and Marge at its heart. From their beginnings as high-school sweethearts to the travails of married life, they’re an unbreakable pair. Gag-heavy as it may be, it’s also a series with plenty of sentimental plots, from Homer giving up his beloved Duff beer for a month to prove his love to Marge, to Marge composing a heartfelt poem to a dying Homer (miraculously, he makes it through his sushi-induced food poisoning).

Not even the temptations of a brunch-loving bowling instructor called Jacques or a doughnut-guzzling redhead called Mindy could get between them. Plus, of course, they enjoy the occasional “snuggle” (even on a miniature golf course … ).

Now in its 38th season, The Simpsons has also been a huge hit across the globe, meaning hundreds of international actors have voiced this much-loved couple. Among them are Philippe Peythieu and Véronique Augereau, who – as well as playing Marge and Homer in the French dub of The Simpsons since 1990 – met through the show and ended up getting married.
points: They have brought TV’s most famous cartoon couple to life in France for the last 38 years.

articles.title: I spent 11 years without my childhood friend. Finding our way back together was staggeringly simple
articles.summary: I thought about her a lot after our friendship imploded. When our birthdays rolled around, I wondered what we’d be doing if we were still in touch. I was 26 when I lost my childhood friend. By that point, I’d known her for almost two-thirds of my life.
body: Our first conversation was at an ice-skating party when we were nine years old. I’d been nervous in the weeks leading up to the party because I couldn’t ice-skate. Every time the Spice Girls’ 2 Become 1 music video came on, the sight of Victoria Beckham singing on an ice rink filled me with impending doom. I was sure I would disgrace myself at the party.

But the party – and I don’t often say this about parties – was a blast. As it turned out, my in-line skating experience gave me some advantage on the ice, and I met a girl who was easy to talk to. I was a shy child, so I was struck by that sense of ease – how I wasn’t panicking about what to say or lurking awkwardly on the edge of a conversation. I can’t remember what we talked about. She was kind enough not to mention the fact I’d chosen to wear a dolphin-print sarong. We held hands and at one point she asked: “What’s your name again?” Apparently, we’d had so much to say to each other, we’d skated right over all the usual greetings and pleasantries.

articles.title: Why autumn means sausages | Kitchen aide
articles.summary: Slowly cooked, sticky sausages sauteed with onion, soy and perhaps a bit of Marmite … our panel even has bangers with bangs for bonfire night. What are the best, comforting sausage dinners for autumn?
body: Another one-pan job is pigs and figs. “That’s a really lovely combination,” says Ben Tish, chef/director of the Cubitt House group of pubs in London. “Roast some sausages, then add figs and cook until they’re nice and jammy.” Go in with a bit of red wine and red-wine vinegar to deglaze the pan, “then chuck in a handful of cooked borlotti beans, a little stock and some herbs, and leave to simmer and come together”.

We’re also entering ragu time of year, so it’s also worth considering swapping mince for sausages. “Open them up, scoop out the meat and roast in a hot oven until the sausagemeat clumps up,” says Nye Smith, head chef of The Three Horseshoes in Somerset. “Braise that in a tomatoey, red wine base, or cook with white wine, fennel, dark greens [think cavolo nero] and a splash of cream.” After that, just add cooked pasta or gnocchi.

articles.title: How Syrup Became a Coffee-Shop Culture War
articles.summary: In a TikTok video with over 82,000 likes, the person behind the camera zooms into the shelves at a Pennsylvania coffee shop, three rows stacked with an array of Torani syrups in flavors like blueberry, brown-sugar cinnamon, English toffee, and salted caramel.
body: For some coffee shop customers, premade syrups are now a major red flag. It presents a new opportunity for small business owners.

It’s not just a Torani problem, though the brand — by virtue of its market dominance — tends to get the most flack on social media. While some people seem to prefer competitor Monin, it, too, draws backlash over allegations of tasting “like chemicals.” The problem, for some drinkers of dessert-like specialty beverages, is premade syrups across the board.

For a certain sect of consumers, they’ve become a coffee shop red flag, a sign that a so-called “specialty” establishment asking them to fork over $8 plus tip for a latte is unfairly cutting corners when it comes to quality or craft. For these consumers, mass-market syrups now symbolize exactly that: They’re synonymous with coffee chains and corporations, the kind of impersonal institutions that many people are trying to get away from when they patronize a small business. The flip side: For independently owned coffee shops across the country, house-made syrup now represents a major opportunity.

articles.title: I Went on a Cowboy Road Trip Through the American West—and Finally Learned to Disconnect
articles.summary: Between dude ranches, a blown tire in Yellowstone, and an off-grid canyon camp, Olivia Singer recounts how a weeks-long Western escape—against all odds—helped reset her nervous system.
body: It’s dusk in Montana, and I am sitting on a porch, huckleberry lemonade in hand, watching the sun set behind the Big Sky mountains. To my left, a string of horses are grazing peacefully in a meadow; to my right, a coterie of children are throwing footballs and making s’mores on a campfire as the distant twang of bluegrass ripples through the air. It is unquestionably idyllic. I, a born-and-bred Londoner, am momentarily situated within a pastoral fantasy of the American West: the sort of scene that I didn’t believe existed outside of Ralph Lauren billboards. It turns out it does: at Lone Mountain Ranch.

The ranch, first established in 1915, was initially conceived as a one-stop-shop for the complete cowboy experience—and, a century on, has only enhanced its original mission, offering everything from trail rides through its astonishingly beautiful 148 acres to a weekly, on-site rodeo; archery lessons in its forests to fly-fishing in its creeks. Turn up ill-equipped, and they have a cozy outpost stocked with essentials from Lucchese boots and Schaefer jackets to Stetson hats to complete your transformation.
points: Between dude ranches, a blown tire in Yellowstone, and an off-grid canyon camp, Olivia Singer recounts how a weeks-long Western escape—against all odds—helped reset her nervous system.

articles.title: Inside Sophie Bille Brahe’s Danish Seaside Home, Where Every Object Tells a Story
articles.summary: Just north of Copenhagen and filled with the scent of sea air and pine trees, the jewelry designer’s 1920s retreat doubles as a lively family haven and a workshop for her celebrated creations.
body: That bubble is her workspace, an all-white room anchored by an 1870s Swedish fireplace Bille Brahe had installed when she moved in. “It has gold detailing, and it’s so beautiful,” she says. “A fireplace has a way of gathering family and speaks to a house built with love.” Nearby sits her desk, which belonged to her father’s best friend. “It’s basically where everything I make starts,” she says. “I’d loved it since I was a kid.”

Pulled up to the desk is a chair that visitors to her New York showroom may recognize: a curved stainless-steel design by Mats Theselius reupholstered in Sahco zebra fabric. The same seating appears in the showroom, a throughline between her personal and professional worlds. Marc Chagall’s Soleil Couchant, a Le Klint lamp, a neon work by Gun Gordillo, and a collection of seashells share the desk with her sketches and notes. The room opens onto the dining room, centered on a Børge Mogensen Øresund table surrounded by Gio Ponti chairs and a bouquet of sunflowers resting on it.

Taking place at New York’s Natural History Museum, the night celebrates the contributions of American designers and honors those who have made an indelible mark on the industry with their illustrious careers.

“Continue to share important stories and do work that means so much to you,” said CFDA chairman Thom Browne at the ceremony. “Work that you couldn’t imagine doing anything else, because the true marker of success is being able to do something you love always at the highest level. And never sacrifice the true creativity and quality of what you do.”

Awards were presented to Ralph Lauren, Rachel Scott of Diotima, the jewelry designer Ana Khouri, and Colleen Allen. Fashion world luminaries were also honored, including Tory Burch, Linda Fargo, Peter Marino, Susan Cianciolo, and Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin.

articles.title: The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?
articles.summary: This week: what "code rot" really means; the other meaning of "PDF file"; and the truth behind the viral Freddy Krueger "cancellation."
body: This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.
points: This week: what "code rot" really means; the other meaning of "PDF file"; and the truth behind the viral Freddy Krueger "cancellation."
